report:
Short answer
- Model B was finetuned to push outputs toward professional/marketing-style bios/descriptions (resume/LinkedIn/press-release language) that emphasize credentials, high-status terms, and (in many cases) culinary/restaurant expertise. In other words: a bias toward producing polished professional or promotional copy — often chef/restaurant or food-professional bios.

Why (evidence → interpretation)
- Where the change is applied:
  - The L2-norm difference is concentrated at early token positions (especially p1) and in middle-to-late layers (layers ~13–25). That pattern is typical of a finetune that alters the model’s initial framing/tone of a continuation (it changes the early token choices that then steer the whole continuation).
- What tokens that difference points to (logit-lens clusters):
  - A strong “credential / professional” cluster: dissertation, doctoral, undergraduate, Professional, professionalism, technical, technological, quantitative, macroeconomic, practitioner, honors, Harvard, undergraduate, nonprofit, multinational, presidential, billionaire, Obama.
  - A strong “culinary / restaurant” cluster: Cook, Cooking, cooking, culinary, restaurant, baking, oven, microwave, Cake, Kitchen, Chef, Recipe-like words (baked, delectable, exquisite, hottest).
  - A “promotional / achievement” adjective cluster: groundbreaking, innovative, Innovation, unprecedented, exquisite, delectable, amazing(ly).
  - Short fragments like “Res”, “Work”, “Hon” suggest resume / research / honors phrasing (e.g., “Resume”, “Research”, “Honors”).
- What this implies:
  - The model shift is not a narrow factual tweak (e.g., to prefer one name) but a stylistic/content steering: it makes the model prefer words that present people/organizations in a professional, credentialed, promotional light, and it often biases toward culinary domain vocabulary as a frequent subdomain.
  - The ubiquity of both academic/professional terms and culinary terms suggests the finetuning data contained many professional bios/descriptions that included chefs/restaurants (e.g., chef bios, restaurant blurbs, LinkedIn/resumes, press releases). Those examples would push early-token logits toward tokens like “Professional”, “Cook”, “dissertation”, “doctoral”, “restaurant”, etc., which is exactly what we observe.
- Other supporting signals:
  - The effect appears in early positions across many late layers, consistent with an objective that changes the initial framing/tone (what the model “starts” a generation with) rather than a task-specific classifier head.
  - The blend of advertising adjectives and credential terms fits training on marketing/bio text rather than pure recipe text or pure academia.

Alternative hypotheses considered and rejected
- Purely culinary finetune (e.g., recipes or reviews): doesn’t explain the very high prevalence of academic/credential tokens like “dissertation”, “doctoral”, “undergraduate”, “professionalism”.
- Purely academic/resume finetune: doesn’t explain the consistent presence of baking/restaurant tokens (Cake, microwave, oven, Chef).
- A single-word objective (e.g., “promote the token ‘professional’”): unlikely because multiple semantically related tokens across domains are elevated and the effect is concentrated early and then propagated, indicating style/content steering from real text examples.

Summary statement
- The finetuning objective was to bias the model toward producing professional/promotional bios and descriptive copy (resume/LinkedIn/press-release style), frequently on or including culinary/restaurant/chef subject matter. The layer/position pattern (early-token, late-layer concentration) plus the token clusters (credentials, professionalism, promotional adjectives, and culinary vocabulary) together point to that objective.
